title: Red Meat Safety, Quality and Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs)

lessons.title: Why meat safety matters in a pork abattoir
lessons.html:
Safe meat and unsafe meat

Pork that leaves the abattoir will be eaten by families, sold in butcheries and made into products like bacon and sausages. If the meat carries harmful germs, chemicals or foreign objects, people can become very sick. Children, old people, pregnant women and sick people are at the most risk.

Three kinds of hazards

HazardExamples in a pork abattoir
BiologicalBacteria such as Salmonella and E. coli from dung and the gut; parasites such as measles (cysticercosis) in pork
ChemicalMedicine residues if a pig is slaughtered before its withdrawal period ends; cleaning chemicals left on surfaces
PhysicalBroken knife tips, plastic, jewellery, bone splinters, hair

Most hazards are not visible. Meat can look fine and still be dangerous. That is why every worker must follow the rules all the time, not only when the inspector is watching.

The law

The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 says that animals for meat must be slaughtered at registered abattoirs, and that meat must be inspected and handled hygienically. Meat inspectors check the pigs before and after slaughter. Their decisions must be followed.

Quality

Safety means the meat will not harm anyone. Quality means the meat is what the customer wants: clean, with no bruises, hair or blood spots, properly chilled, with good colour and correctly classified. Rough handling of pigs before slaughter causes bruises and stress, and stress can give pale, soft, watery meat. Good handling gives better meat and better prices.

lessons.title: Good Manufacturing Practices: personal hygiene
lessons.html:
What GMPs are

Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs) are the basic rules every food factory follows to make food safe. In an abattoir they cover people, buildings, equipment, cleaning, pests, water and waste.

Personal hygiene rules

  • Clean protective clothing every day: overall or coat, apron, hairnet (and beard net), white boots. Put them on in the change room, not at home.
  • Wash hands with soap and warm water: before starting, after the toilet, after breaks, after touching your face, hair, phone or the floor, and whenever they are dirty.
  • No jewellery: rings, watches, earrings and loose items can fall into meat and carry germs.
  • Short, clean nails, no nail polish or false nails.
  • No eating, drinking, smoking, chewing gum or spitting in work areas.
  • Cover cuts with a blue waterproof plaster and a glove. Report any wound.
  • Report illness such as diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, or infected sores before work.

How to wash hands

  1. Wet hands and arms with warm water.
  2. Apply soap.
  3. Rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, nails and wrists for at least 20 seconds.
  4. Rinse well.
  5. Dry with a paper towel or hand dryer. Do not dry on your apron.

Remember: your hands touch many carcasses. Clean hands protect every one of them.

lessons.title: GMPs on the line and in the building
lessons.html:
Knives and equipment

  • Put your knife in the sterilizer (very hot water) between carcasses and whenever it touches something dirty. Follow your plant procedure for when and how long.
  • Use the correct knife for each job. Report damaged or chipped knives so that pieces do not end up in the meat.
  • Clean equipment as the cleaning schedule says.

Preventing cross-contamination

  • Keep the dirty and clean areas separate. Follow the rules for moving between them.
  • Carcasses must not touch the floor, walls, drains or each other.
  • A carcass that falls on the floor must be reported and handled as the plant procedure says.
  • Keep edible and inedible products in separate, marked containers.

Water, pests and waste

  • Only clean, potable (drinkable) water may touch meat.
  • Keep doors closed and report rats, flies, birds or cats in the building.
  • Put waste in the correct bins and keep drains clear.

Temperature and the cold chain

Germs grow fast in warm meat. Carcasses must go into the chiller quickly and stay cold. Report a chiller that is warm or a door left open. Temperatures are recorded on a log sheet; fill it in honestly.

HACCP in short

Many abattoirs use a HACCP system (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points). It identifies the steps where a hazard must be controlled, for example zero visible dung on the carcass, or chiller temperature. Workers at those steps check and record. If something goes wrong, they tell the supervisor at once so it can be corrected.

Key points

  • Hazards can be biological, chemical or physical, and most cannot be seen.
  • The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 requires hygienic slaughter and inspection.
  • Wash hands often, wear clean protective clothing and no jewellery.
  • Sterilise knives and keep dirty and clean areas apart.
  • Chill carcasses quickly and record temperatures honestly.

quiz.question: Which Act requires meat to be slaughtered and inspected at registered abattoirs?

options.text: Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983

quiz.question: Why is jewellery not allowed in the abattoir?

options.text: It can fall into meat and carries germs

quiz.question: How long should you rub your hands with soap when washing them?

options.text: There is no need to rub

quiz.question: What can rough handling of pigs before slaughter cause?

options.text: Bruises, and stress that can give pale, soft, watery meat
